passages.text: Pathological evaluation of the pathogenesis of diabetes mellitus and diabetic peripheral neuropathy
Abstract

Currently, there are more than 10 million patients with diabetes mellitus in Japan. Therefore, the need to explore the pathogenesis of diabetes and the complications leading to its cure is becoming increasingly urgent. Pathological examination of pancreatic tissues from patients with type 2 diabetes reveals a decrease in the volume of beta cells because of a combination of various stresses. In human type 2 diabetes, islet amyloid deposition is a unique pathological change characterized by proinflammatory macrophage (M1) infiltration into the islets. The pathological changes in the pancreas with islet amyloid were different according to clinical factors, which suggests that type 2 diabetes can be further subclassified based on islet pathology. On the other hand, diabetic peripheral neuropathy is the most frequent diabetic complication. In early diabetic peripheral neuropathy, M1 infiltration in the sciatic nerve evokes oxidative stress or attenuates retrograde axonal transport, as clearly demonstrated by in vitro live imaging. Furthermore, islet parasympathetic nerve density and beta cell volume were inversely correlated in type 2 diabetic Goto‐Kakizaki rats, suggesting that diabetic peripheral neuropathy itself may contribute to the decrease in beta cell volume. These findings suggest that the pathogenesis of diabetes mellitus and diabetic peripheral neuropathy may be interrelated.

DIABETES AND ITS COMPLICATIONS

Currently, the number of patients with diabetes mellitus is rapidly increasing in modern society, including Japan, where there are more than 10 million patients. Diabetes is mainly classified into type 1 diabetes and type 2 diabetes (Figure 1a); among them, type 2 diabetes is the most common (>85% of all patients with diabetes). Unfortunately, no radical treatment for both type 1 and type 2 diabetes has been established. Because of its rapidly increasing prevalence, it is urgently necessary to explore the pathogenesis of type 2 diabetes and the complications leading to its cure.

Pathophysiology of diabetes mellitus and its complications. (a) Type 1 diabetes develops when beta cells are destroyed by autoimmune mechanisms and thereafter, insulin secretion is depleted. On the other hand, type 2 diabetes has a variety of pathological states. In Japanese, the main pathogenesis is deficient insulin secretion from beta cells, while in Westerners, the main pathogenesis is insulin resistance due to obesity. (b) Diabetic complications can occur regardless of whether it is type 1 or type 2 diabetes mellitus. Their complications include MASLD in the liver, macrovascular complications such as atherosclerosis and myocardial infarction, microvascular complications such as nephropathy, retinopathy, and neuropathy, and cancer such as pancreatic ductal cancer and uterine cancer. MASLD, metabolic dysfunction‐associated fatty liver disease.

Type 2 diabetes is a complex and heterogeneous disease influenced by genetic factors accompanied by environmental factors. The pathophysiology of type 2 diabetes can be divided into two major categories (Figure 1a). The first category involves significant insulin resistance in peripheral tissue, such as fatty tissue and muscle tissue. This type of diabetes is mainly associated with a high body mass index (BMI; average 27.5) in white type 2 diabetes patients but not in Japanese type 2 diabetes patients (average BMI 23.4). In this type of diabetes, insulin secretion is preserved; rather, hypersecretion occurs, resulting in hyperinsulinemia. The other category involves insufficient insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells. The pathophysiology of Japanese type 2 diabetes patients is assumed to involve impaired insulin secretion rather than insulin resistance. Diabetes is thought to develop with the involvement of these two pathophysiologies to varying degrees depending on the patient. Because a deficit of insulin secretion in beta cells can be associated with the pathological changes of beta cells, these findings may suggest that the pathological changes in beta cells can vary among patients. If a new classification for type 2 diabetes can be generated according to the pathological changes in beta cells, it would be useful to develop new tailor‐made therapies for type 2 diabetes.

Diabetic complications determine the prognosis of patients. The characteristic complications of diabetes are microvascular complications such as nephropathy, retinopathy, and neuropathy (Figure 1b). In addition, macrovascular complications, such as acute myocardial infarction (AMI), cerebral infarction, and periodontal disease, are widely known complications of diabetes mellitus. Metabolic dysfunction associated with steatotic liver disease N is known as a diabetic complication. Furthermore, in recent years, diabetes mellitus has become an important risk factor for carcinoma onset and development in specific organs, such as pancreatic cancer, colon cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, uterine cancer, and nasopharyngeal cancer. Therefore, these carcinomas are also considered to be complications of diabetes mellitus. Among them, diabetic peripheral neuropathy, which is a type of diabetic neuropathy, is the most frequent and earliest complication. However, radical treatment for diabetic peripheral neuropathy has not been established to date. Similar to the pathophysiology of diabetes itself, there is an urgent need to explore novel pathophysiologies directly leading to new therapies for diabetic peripheral neuropathy.
Pathological exploration in diabetes

As mentioned above, diabetes mellitus is a hormonal ataxia primarily caused by an absolute or relative deficiency of insulin. Therefore, because the diagnosis of diabetes is based on fasting blood glucose and hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) levels, biopsies of the pancreas or fatty tissue are rarely performed. In contrast, liver biopsies are sometimes performed to confirm metabolic dysfunction‐associated steatohepatitis. Biopsies are not performed for the diagnosis of nephropathy except for special cases. In diabetic neuropathy, the gold standard for diagnosis is to measure nerve conduction velocity and amplitude via electromyography; however, this method is not commonly used except in situations where the clinical features are atypical, the diagnosis is unclear, or a different etiology is suspected. Instead, several simple electrophysiological testing devices have been developed and are currently being tested for their usefulness. Biopsies of the peroneal nerve and skin of the leg have been performed in the past for diagnosis but are no longer performed due to their invasive nature. In contrast, basic research on diabetes and its complications has been performed based on pathological, physiological, biochemical, molecular biological, and combinations of these approaches. In particular, the pathophysiology of diabetes has been extensively explored with pathological techniques using various organs of model animals, autopsy tissue, surgical specimens, and biopsy skin. Pathological changes in human pancreatic beta cells have been studied via autopsy and surgical resection of the pancreas. In such cases, the use of surgical specimens is not recommended because most of them are cancer‐associated specimens, which may influence the islet pathology, and because the prevalence of the pancreatic head is high, in which the islet structure is different from that of the body and tail of the pancreas.
PATHOLOGICAL CHANGES IN BETA CELLS IN NONOBESE TYPE 2 DIABETIC GOTO KAKIZAKI (GK) RATS

The GK rat is a spontaneous nonobese model of type 2 diabetes characterized by low insulin secretion, similar to that in Asian patients with type 2 diabetes (Figure 2a). This model was established by selective breeding of hyperglycemic Wistar rats at Hirosaki University. The islet pathology in this model shows a progressive decrease in beta cell mass (Figure 2b). A diabetic state increases oxidative stress in the islets, which causes beta cell death or degradation (Figure 2c). Because reactive oxidative species can generally be generated in mitochondria, mitochondria were evaluated in detail. Electron microscopy was used to evaluate the mitochondrial morphology of beta cells in GK rats and revealed swelling and disrupted crista structure. Compared with that in Wistar rats, the mitochondrial membrane potential in response to high sucrose stimulation in isolated islets was significantly attenuated. Serradas et al. reported a progressive reduction in mitochondrial DNA in beta cells of GK rats. These findings suggest that mitochondrial deficits can be a key factor in morphological changes in beta cells in GK rats. In addition to mitochondrial dysfunction, macrophages significantly infiltrate the surrounding islets. Thus, islet inflammation would be involved in the reduction of beta cells eliciting oxidative stress in GK rats.

Goto‐Kakizaki rats and its morphological changes of beta cells. (a) GK rats are smaller than their original non‐diabetic counterparts, Wistar rats. (b) Compared to Wistar rats, islets in GK rats are star‐shaped and fragmented, and beta cell volume is decreased, visualized by tetra‐immunohistochemistry for islet hormones. (c) Previous studies have shown that hyperglycemia in GK rats causes oxidative stress evaluated by 8‐OHdG staining, macrophage infiltration of islets evaluated by Iba‐I staining, abnormal beta cell mitochondrial morphology, and a decrease in the number of vagal pancreatic branch ends in the islets evaluated by VachT staining (yellow arrows). GK rats, Goto‐Kakizaki rats; VachT, vesicular acetylcholine transporter.
Pathological changes in islet beta cells in human specimens

There were no arguments about beta cell volume in human type 2 diabetes patients until approximately 2000 because no evaluation was performed with immunostaining. We first reported a significant reduction in beta cell volume of up to 30% in pathological examination of pancreatic tissue from autopsy patients with type 2 diabetes. Similar to that in GK rats, oxidative stress induced by hyperglycemia was increased in beta cells in type 2 diabetic rats. Furthermore, a combination of oxidative stress, autophagy failure, and endoplasmic reticulum stress was involved in the decrease in beta cells in human type 2 diabetes patients. Because the density of the beta cell volume was coordinately correlated with the HbA1c level, a hyperglycemic state is also a significant factor for the reduction in beta cell volume in human type 2 diabetes patients. In human type 2 diabetes patients, islet amyloid deposition is known to be a unique pathological change. Islet amyloid is a type of local amyloidosis that consists of islet amyloid polypeptide (IAPP) protein, also known as amylin. IAPP is cosecreted with insulin from beta cells. Amyloids are toxic fibrils organized as dynamic cross‐β‐sheet structures. Previous reports have shown that toxic fibrils of amyloid are harmful to beta cells. In line with these results, beta cell volume was markedly reduced in patients with islet amyloid deposition compared to that in nonamyloid deposit diabetic patients (Figure 3a). IAPP impairs the survival of beta cells in isolated islets by releasing cytokines such as IL‐1β and IL‐63. In our study, proinflammatory macrophage (M1) infiltration was significantly increased in islets with amyloid deposition in type 2 diabetes patients. Thus, amyloid deposition significantly changed the islet pathology of type 2 diabetes patients.

Pathological classification of type 2 diabetes based on the clinical characteristics of amyloid deposition in the islets. (a) Compared with the new classification of diabetes mellitus suggested by Ahlqvist et al., the severe insulin resistance type and the Japanese autopsy cases of type 2 diabetes mellitus complicated with macroangiopathy such as AMI and renal failure, and the mild age‐related type and the Japanese autopsy cases of type 2 diabetes mellitus with elderly onset can be clinically homologous, respectively. In addition to those types, mildly obese Japanese patients show prominent islet amyloid deposition. Islet amyloid deposition induces a severe decrease in beta cell volume and no compensatory increase in alpha cell volume. In addition, it promotes infiltration of M1 macrophages into the islets. (b) Double immunohistochemistry for CD31 and Chromogranin A clearly visualized the increase in the number of capillaries in the islet of DM + AMI. Type IV collagen was the most deposited of all groups in the islets of DM + AMI. AMI, acute myocardial infarction; DM, diabetes mellitus; M1, proinflammatory macrophages.
NEW SUBCLASSIFICATION OF TYPE 2 DIABETES BASED ON THE PATHOLOGICAL CHANGES IN THE ISLETS

Because the etiologies of type 2 diabetes are not homogeneous but rather heterogeneous, further subclassifications are being made for the establishment of better treatment methods rather than simply classifying type 2 diabetes into one type. The most popular subclassification was conducted by Swedish investigators (Figure 3a); they classified type 2 diabetes into five subgroups, namely, the autoimmune‐based type (type 1 diabetes), insulin‐deficient type, aging‐related type, obesity‐related type, and insulin‐resistant type, based on glutamic acid decarboxylase antibody, age, BMI, HbA1c, homeostasis model assessment of beta cell function, and homeostasis model assessment of insulin resistance. Among these, they found that a group of type 2 diabetes patients with severe insulin resistance developed a high incidence of chronic kidney disease and cardiovascular events with poor prognosis. Patients with severe insulin deficiency have the highest risk of early diabetic retinopathy and neuropathy. Two studies employed alternative approach clustering variants and multiple glycemic and nonglycemic traits using genetic clustering, which subclassified type 2 diabetes into a set of five broadly overlapping genetic clusters: two clusters related to decreased beta cell function (e.g., MTNR1B, TCF7L2, HNF1A, SLC30A8, reduced disposition index, increased proinsulin adjusted for insulin levels; and ARAP1/STARD10, reduced proinsulin adjusted for insulin levels) and three related to mechanisms of insulin resistance, mediated through (1) obesity (e.g., FTO, MC4R, NRXN3, increased percentage body fat, BMI); (2) abnormal fat distribution or “lipodystrophy” (e.g., PPARG, IRS1, KLF14, increased fasting insulin, triglycerides, reduced BMI); and (3) impaired liver/lipid metabolism (e.g., GCKR, PNPLA3, TM6SF2, reduced triglycerides). Nevertheless, the changes in islet pathology in the aforementioned subgroups of patients with type 2 diabetes remain unclear. The pathological changes in islets may differ according to the subgroup of patients with type 2 diabetes, reflecting the pathogenesis of each subgroup.
Pathological subclassification based on the islet amyloidosis

Known risk factors for islet amyloid deposition include obesity, aging, and macrovascular disease, and it is not clear that there are pathological differences among the subjects with islet amyloid deposition elicited by different etiologies (Figure 3a). We first evaluated how aging affects islet amyloid deposition in type 2 diabetes mellitus. Type 2 diabetes mellitus in the elderly can be divided into two types: those who develop diabetes in middle age and become elderly and those who develop diabetes for the first time in old age. The former type is considered as conventional type 2 diabetes. The latter type, on the other hand, is assumed to be a specific type of type 2 diabetes. Thus, the pathology of elderly‐onset diabetes is supposed to be different from that of middle‐aged diabetes. (1) The influence of genetic factors is less pronounced in elderly onset type 2 diabetes patients than in middle‐aged individuals. (2) Insulin resistance due to sarcopenia (a progressive and generalized skeletal muscle disorder involving the accelerated loss of muscle mass and function) triggers the onset of the disease. (3) Individuals with diabetes are prone to hypoglycemia. Although these findings suggest that pathological changes in the islet in elderly diabetic patients may be involved, a detailed pathological exploration of the islet has not been performed. We evaluated the pathological findings of pancreas specimens dissected from autopsied patients with diabetes onset after 75 years of age. Pathological examination of elderly diabetic subjects revealed severe amyloid deposition in the islets with a severe reduction in beta cell volume. Furthermore, there is a high frequency of pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia with atrophy of the pancreatic parenchyma and interstitial fibrosis. Because these pathological findings were not evident in the elderly with diabetes in middle age, these findings could reflect the pathophysiology of elderly individuals with type 2 diabetes, such as high insulin resistance.

We also evaluated pancreas specimens dissected from diabetic subjects with macrovascular disease, such as AMI (Figure 3b). Patients with type 2 diabetes with AMI had a greater incidence of kidney failure than did subjects with type 2 diabetes without AMI. According to the pathological analysis, the intraislet vasculature dramatically changed with a high incidence of islet amyloid deposition. The vascular diameter decreased while the vascular number significantly increased. The thickness of the vascular basement membrane in the subjects with AMI was significantly greater than that in the subjects with type 2 diabetes without AMI. In contrast, the degree to which pericytes covered the vessels was significantly less than that in type 2 diabetes patients without AMI. These findings could suggest that macrovascular failure can cause intraislet microvascular damage in type 2 diabetes patients, resulting in amyloid deposition and beta cell failure.

Thus, islet amyloid deposition and intra‐ductal neoplasia were characteristic in elderly‐onset diabetes mellitus, while microvascular lesions and amyloid deposition within the islets were present in type 2 diabetes mellitus complicated by macrovascular disease. These suggest that islet pathology can be different depending on the etiology of diabetes. According to the clinical manifestations reported by Ahlqvist et al., elderly onset type 2 diabetes can correspond to the aging‐related type, and type 2 diabetes complicated with AMI can correspond to the severe insulin resistance type (a high incidence of renal failure and a possible presence of insulin resistance) (Figure 3a). Thus, pathological findings of the islet can further reveal the mechanism underlying clinical classification. These findings suggest that type 2 diabetes can also be further subclassified based on islet pathology; this may be applicable to future tailor‐made therapies.
Diabetic peripheral neuropathy, the most prevalent and earliest complication of diabetes

Diabetes elicits several types of neuropathy. Although several types of classification have been suggested, classification, according to PK.Thomas, is most widely used for general purposes. Thomas classified diabetic neuropathy into six types. First, diabetic neuropathy can be divided into systemic and localized neuropathy. Systematic neuropathy includes diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Diabetic peripheral neuropathy is subclassified into distal symmetric sensory (motor) neuropathy and autonomic neuropathy. Localized neuropathy is subclassified into mononeuropathy, lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy, entrapment neuropathy, chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy, and central nervous system disorder. Diabetic peripheral neuropathy is the most prevalent type of neuropathy. Approximately 30% of diabetic peripheral neuropathy patients are symptomatic at the time of diabetes diagnosis, but electrophysiological abnormalities are present in almost 90% of patients. This suggests that almost all patients with diabetes mellitus have diabetic peripheral neuropathy at diagnosis, even if they are asymptomatic. The prevalent symptoms are numbness, pain, and hyperalgesia of the bilateral toes. The obvious symptoms gradually disappeared, and the patient developed hypoesthesia because of sensory loss. This sensory loss can lead to ulcer formation in the legs. Without strict control of hyperglycemia or local wounds, the worst‐case scenario is amputation of the foot. Thus, sensory deficits in diabetic peripheral neuropathy patients are directly related to quality of life. On the other hand, the symptoms of autonomic neuropathy are orthostatic hypotension, diarrhea, constipation, and neurogenic bladder. When cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy such as lethal arrhythmias and painless myocardial infarctions occur, the risk of sudden death increases. These findings suggest that the manifestation of autonomic neuropathy is directly related to patient prognosis. Unfortunately, because there is no curative treatment for diabetic peripheral neuropathy, there is an urgent need to elucidate novel mechanisms directly related to its treatment.
Pathological alterations of peripheral nervous systems elicited by diabetic peripheral neuropathy

Diabetic peripheral neuropathy mainly affects the peripheral nervous system, which can be divided into motor and sensory nervous systems. They relay information afferently and efferently, respectively. Sensory peripheral nerves begin in the dorsal root ganglion (DRG) of the spinal cord, which is more than 1 meter long in the foot (Figure 4). The peripheral nervous system is maintained and supported by glia, Schwann cells, blood vessels, and the interstitium. The sensory peripheral nervous system is composed of unmyelinated C fibers and myelinated A‐δ fibers called small‐diameter nerve fibers, and A‐β fibers called myelinated large‐diameter nerve fibers. In diabetic peripheral neuropathy, various sites of the peripheral nervous system, including DRG neurons, nerve fibers, and Schwann cells, are injured (Figure 4). Pathological evaluation shows the atrophy of DRG ganglion cells, degeneration of large nerve fibers, thickness of vascular walls of intranerve fiber vessels, and loss of small nerve fibers in the epidermis. It is generally accepted that diabetic peripheral neuropathy is a retrograde neuropathy caused by metabolic factors, mainly hyperglycemia. In the early stages of diabetic peripheral neuropathy, small‐diameter nerves within the epidermis or cornea can be first reduced. In our study of the pain thresholds of small nerves caused by electrical stimulation in a health examination cohort, pain thresholds were found to decrease at normal high HbA1c levels (5.8%−6.4%), which is not diagnosed as diabetes or impaired fasting glucose. These findings indicate that diabetic peripheral neuropathy may develop from a state of minor impaired glucose metabolism with pathological alterations.

Anatomy of the peripheral sensory nervous system and pathological changes in diabetic peripheral neuropathy. (a) The peripheral sensory nervous system is innervated by DRG neurons from the dorsal horn of the spinal cord to the end of the foot. The length of the peripheral nervous system is over one meter. Therefore, in DPN, abnormal glucose metabolism and associated dyslipidemia cause accumulation of damage to nerve fiber endings, resulting in a form of retrograde neuropathy. (b) Pathological evaluation reveals the reduction of small nerve fibers in the epidermis of DPN (red arrows). Atrophy, degeneration, partial demyelination of axons, and hyalinized thickness of small vessel wall (red arrow) occur in large diameter myelinated nerves in the sural nerve of DPN. The ganglion cells of the DRG show atrophy and reduce due to metabolic insults in DPN. DPN, diabetic peripheral neuropathy; DRG, dorsal root ganglion.
DIABETIC PERIPHERAL NEUROPATHY AND ANTIDIABETIC THERAPY

Large clinical studies, such as the Diabetes Control and Complications Trial, have demonstrated that strict glycemic control reduces disease onset and progression of peripheral neruopathy. Therefore, blood glycemic control has long been considered the most important treatment for diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Currently, many antidiabetic medicines are used clinically for treating type 2 diabetes. Researchers expect that these medications have a direct protective effect on peripheral nerve tissue in addition to hypoglycemic effects. In particular, dipeptidyl peptidase‐4 (DPP‐4) inhibitors, which are widely used in Japan, and glucagon‐like peptide‐1 (GLP‐1) agonists have been shown to have protective effects on diabetic peripheral neuropathy in basic research. We demonstrated that a DPP‐4 inhibitor could ameliorate diabetic peripheral neuropathy via the resolution of insulin resistance in the peripheral nerves in a DPN model of type 1 diabetes and type 2 diabetes. Unfortunately, the effects of DPP‐4 inhibitors and GLP‐1 agonists are still controversial in actual clinical practice. We found that simultaneous administration of a sodium−glucose transporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor, which is considered to have a strong hypoglycemic effect and no direct effect on nerves, markedly improved intraepidermal small nerve density and intrapancreatic islet parasympathetic branch density, although single administration of DPP‐4 inhibitors was also effective against diabetic peripheral neuropathy. These findings suggest that multiple administrations of antidiabetic compounds with different mechanisms may be more effective at improving peripheral nerve function than single drug administration, even in clinical settings.
Suggested mechanisms of diabetic peripheral neuropathy development and progression

As mentioned above, the onset and progression of diabetic peripheral neuropathy are multifactorial (Figure 5). Previous studies have postulated that hyperglycemia and dyslipidemia elicit the activation of the polyol pathway, oxidative stress, advanced glycation end products (AGEs) and its receptor for AGEs (RAGE) signaling, abnormal activation of protein kinase C (PKC), inflammation, decreased neurotrophic factors, and insulin resistance in the peripheral nervous system in diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Furthermore, the thickness of the microvasculature of intranerve tissues can cause ischemia. It is believed that a combination of these factors is involved in the onset and progression of diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Among these pathways, only inhibitors of aldose reductase (ARI), the rate‐limiting enzyme of the polyol pathway, and alpha‐lipoic acid, an antioxidant stress drug, have been applied in clinical practice. The polyol pathway is a subpathway of the glycolytic system, which normally receives less than 5% of the glucose entering the glycolytic pathway. Once hyperglycemia occurs, large amounts of glucose enter and activate the pathway. As a result of polyol pathway activation, oxidative stress, increased intracellular osmotic pressure, and increased AGE production induce cellular injury in the peripheral nervous system, which promotes the onset and progression of diabetic peripheral neuropathy. ARI, however, is not a panacea, and its efficacy has been shown to be insufficient in patients with poor glycemic control and an advanced stage of diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Alpha‐lipoic acid, which is on the market in Japan as a supplement, is not expected to have a curative effect on diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Some of the other pathways, such as inhibitors of PKC, have been clinically investigated, but none of them have reached clinical application due to the lack of clinical significance. Although the AGE‐RAGE pathway has been assumed to be involved in the pathogenesis of diabetic peripheral neuropathy, the findings are not conclusive. Regarding the involvement of insulin signaling in diabetic peripheral neuropathy, a nerve‐specific knockout mouse of the insulin receptor did not show a neuropathic phenotype, while an insulin receptor and insulin‐like growth factor I (IGF‐1) receptor double knockout mouse specific to peripheral nerves showed impaired Schwann cell function. The IGF‐1 receptor also acts as a receptor for insulin. Therefore, it is possible that IGF‐I receptor signaling is activated by insulin instead of the insulin receptor in insulin receptor knockout mice, but its involvement in diabetic peripheral neuropathy is still inconclusive.

Currently envisioned pathology of diabetic peripheral neuropathy. In addition to hyperglycemia, other known risk factors for DPN include dyslipidemia, hypertension, and worsening lifestyle habits such as smoking and obesity. A combination of these clinical factors can induce activation of the polyol pathway, formation of advanced glycation end‐products, activation of their receptor RAGE, abnormal activation of PKC, inflammation, oxidative stress, dysfunction of intracellular signals, and deposition of glucosamine in the peripheral nervous system. It is believed that a combination of these pathological conditions is involved in the onset and progression of DPN. Thus, DPN is a multifactorial disease. DPN, diabetic peripheral neuropathy; PKC, protein kinase C; RAGE, receptor or advanced glycation end‐products.
Exploration of novel mechanisms of diabetic peripheral neuropathy pathogenesis

The mechanism of diabetic peripheral neuropathy differs between the early and advanced stages. Especially in the advanced stages, ARI is less effective, and there is no established treatment other than symptomatic therapy. Recent advances in analytical methods have enabled comprehensive analysis of mRNA expression using microarrays or RNA sequences as well as metabolites and proteins. We hypothesized that the activation of other metabolic pathways may be the reason for ARI failure during the progression of diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Comprehensive metabolomic analysis of the sciatic nerves of 16‐week‐old wild‐type and aldose reductase knockout mice was performed. We detected the accumulation of glucosamine, a metabolite of the hexosamine pathway, which is one of the collateral pathways of glycolysis, in the sciatic nerves of streptozotocin (STZ) induced diabetic mice (Figure 5). Glucosamine is well‐known as a supplement for joint pain. However, excessive intake of glucosamine may cause insulin resistance. In a study using Schwann cell lines and mice, glucosamine was found to cause overactivation of hexokinase, a metabolic enzyme for glucose and glucosamine, resulting in decreased glucose metabolism and excessive ATP consumption, which in turn leads to dysfunction of the peripheral nervous system. This finding suggests that the modification of glucosamine metabolism may lead to a new therapeutic option for advanced stages of diabetic peripheral neuropathy.
Iwaki Health Promotion Project conducted in Hirosaki and small‐fiber neuropathy

The Iwaki Health Promotion Project is a health checkup‐based health promotion study that has been conducted at Hirosaki University for more than 15 years. The Iwaki Project targets approximately 1000 residents of the town of Iwaki in the suburbs of Hirosaki city each year. The Iwaki Project evaluates more than 3000 noninvasive items each year. The pain threshold of the intraepidermal nerve terminal (PINT) method is a method of selectively stimulating A‐δ and C‐fibers in the epidermis with a weak electric current. This evokes pain perceived by the subject. This procedure can be used to evaluate the function of small fibers quantitatively. The PINT in the Iwaki project revealed that glucose metabolic factors such as blood glucose level and HbA1c and metabolic syndrome factors such as dyslipidemia, hypertension, and obesity are involved in the deterioration of the PINT index. In addition, as novel findings, the deterioration of the PINT index was associated with normal high HbA1c levels (5.9%−6.4%), high levels of urinary 8‐hydroxyloxy‐2′‐deoxyguanosine, and high levels of lipopolysaccharide‐binding protein (LBP) in the blood. Since blood LBP levels are known to be closely related to lipopolysaccharide release by Gram‐negative rods, the intestinal and oral microflora were further examined. A decrease in the ratio of the Bacteroides genus in the intestinal microflora was significantly related to a decrease in the PINT index, regardless of glucose metabolism status. On the other hand, changes in the oral microflora were not related to the PINT index. These results indicate that the PINT index is closely related to factors such as diabetes and metabolic syndrome, while it can be altered by various factors other than known factors, such as changes in the intestinal microflora. Furthermore, it is generally known that blood LBP levels are closely related to macrophage activation. Although the involvement of macrophages in peripheral nerves in diabetic peripheral neuropathy has been reported based on the results of basic experiments, the detailed mechanism has not yet been elucidated.
Macrophage infiltration in diabetic peripheral neuropathy patients with type 2 diabetes

Macrophage infiltration in peripheral nerves is considered one of the pathophysiologies of diabetic peripheral neuropathy. On the other hand, macrophage infiltration in the early stage of diabetic peripheral neuropathy has been reported to be a reparative response to sciatic nerve injury. Therefore, its impact on the pathogenesis of diabetic peripheral neuropathy is unclear. Xanthine oxidase is the rate‐limiting enzyme in uric acid metabolism. In addition, xanthine oxidase is involved in the activation of macrophages via the generation of reactive oxygen species. Activation of xanthine oxidase could polarize them into M1 macrophages and increase the oxidative stress and the production of cytokines. Blood xanthine oxidase activity is elevated in type 2 diabetes complicated with peripheral neuropathy (Figure 6). It has been reported that administration of allopurinol, an inhibitor of xanthine oxidase, improved symptoms of experimental diabetic peripheral neuropathy. However, the mechanism underlying this improvement is unknown. Therefore, we administered topiroxostat, an inhibitor of xanthine oxidase, to db/db mice, an animal model of obese type 2 diabetes, to evaluate the role of xanthine oxidase in diabetic peripheral neuropathy. We found that the administration of topiroxostat could improve nerve conduction velocity and intraepidermal small nerve fiber density. Macrophage infiltration in the sciatic nerve reached a maximum at eight weeks of age and, thereafter, gradually decreased, whereas the M1/anti‐inflammatory macrophage (M2) ratio gradually increased. Topiroxostat treatment significantly suppressed M1 macrophage infiltration in the sciatic nerves of db/db mice. When the effect of xanthine oxidase on macrophages was examined in vitro, xanthine oxidase in the medium significantly polarized macrophages to the M1 phenotype. Topiroxostat inhibited the polarization of macrophages toward the M1 phenotype. Furthermore, xanthine oxidase in the medium significantly inhibited neurite sprouting in primary cultured DRG neurons, while topiroxostat treatment significantly improved neurite sprouting. These results indicate that factors in the blood, such as xanthine oxidase, are important in the pathogenesis of diabetic peripheral neuropathy through the activation of macrophages and injury to neurons. Consequently, inflammation, such as macrophage infiltration of peripheral nerves, as observed in the Iwaki study, was also pronounced in the early stages of peripheral neuropathy in db/db mice, which results in pathogenesis through oxidative stress and other factors.

Involvement of activation of XO in the blood in the onset and progression of the early stage of diabetic peripheral neuropathy in type 2 diabetes mellitus. Type 2 diabetes shows activation of XO in the blood, which induces the generation of ROS. This evokes infiltration of M1 macrophages in the sciatic nerve, resulting in the induction of cytokine secretion or oxidative stress. Concurrently, ROS generated by activation of XO directly can injure ganglion cells of DRG. XO inhibitor treatment reduces XO activity, suppresses M1 macrophage infiltration, and reduces oxidative stress, resulting in suppression of the development of DPN. DPN, diabetic peripheral neuropathy; DRG, dorsal root ganglion; IENFD, intraepidermal nerve fiber density; M1, proinflammatory macrophages; ROS, reactive oxygen species; XO, xanthin oxidase.
Macrophage infiltration in diabetic peripheral neuropathy of type 1 diabetes

AGEs are formed when sugars and proteins react in a nonenzymatic manner. There is a chemical linkage between the carbonyl groups and the amino group to form Schiff bases and then Amadori compounds, followed by irreversible dehydration, condensation, and cross‐linking, resulting in heterogeneous derivatives termed AGEs. In particular, the involvement of AGEs in diabetic complications has been reported. In diabetic peripheral neuropathy, methoglyoxal is deposited in the epidermis in painful neuropathy, which activates the voltage‐gated sodium channel Nav1.8 and induces pain. On the other hand, AGEs are known to evoke inflammatory reactions and tissue damage through the activation of their receptor, RAGE. Nevertheless, the involvement of AGE‐RAGE signaling in diabetic peripheral neuropathy is not conclusive. We evaluated the involvement of AGE‐RAGE signaling using RAGE knockout mice. With the induction of type 1 diabetes in RAGE knockout mice, the reduction in nerve conduction velocity was ameliorated. Macrophage infiltration in the sciatic nerve was evaluated after eight weeks of diabetes. There was marked M1 macrophage infiltration in the diabetic group. Interestingly, M1 macrophage infiltration was not increased, while M2 macrophage infiltration was markedly increased in RAGE‐knockout mice with diabetes. Concurrently, maintenance of insulin sensitivity in the sciatic nerve, improvement of retrograde axonal transport, and inhibition of DRG neuron atrophy were evident in diabetic RAGE‐knockout mice. To confirm the involvement of macrophages in the attenuation of symptoms in diabetic peripheral neuropathy and the underlying mechanisms in RGAE knockout mice, a bone marrow transplantation model of RAGE knockout mice complicated with diabetic peripheral neuropathy was used, and peripheral nerves were pathologically examined (Figure 7a). These results were similar to those of RAGE‐knockout mice, suggesting that RAGE expressed on macrophages is involved in the pathogenesis of diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Furthermore, retrograde axonal transport was examined by coculturing isolated DRG neurons with macrophages via live imaging. Retrograde axonal transport in neurons was markedly interrupted when they were cocultured with M1 macrophages. These results suggest that RAGE on macrophages is important for the polarization of macrophages toward the M1 phenotype. M1 macrophage infiltration induces insulin resistance and dysfunction of retrograde axonal transport in the sciatic nerve; this may be an important mechanism of diabetic peripheral neuropathy, similar to the dysfunction of the neuronal cells themselves evoked by metabolic disorders (Figure 7b).

The association between beta cell deficit and diabetic peripheral neuropathy

Our results indicate that inflammatory response is a common pathway for both reduced beta cell volume in type 2 diabetes and diabetic neuropathy. Is there another pathophysiological condition that directly links these two pathological conditions? Beta cell proliferation is known to be related to the autonomic nervous system. In particular, signals transmitted via the vagus nerve are known to be regulators of both beta cell function and proliferation. Neural input from the liver to the pancreas via branches of the vagus nerve stimulates the secretion of neurotransmitters from nerve endings, leading to the proliferation of beta cells. These findings suggest that functional vagal innervation with a sufficient number of nerve endings is essential for maintaining beta cell volume. On the other hand, it was inconclusive whether the autonomic density of pancreatic islets is reduced by diabetic peripheral neuropathy and is thus related to the reduction in beta cell volume. In GK rats, the density of the parasympathetic nerve endings labeled with vesicular acetylcholine transporter antibody was significantly reduced in line with the reduction in the Ki67 index and volume of beta cells (Figure 2c). More interestingly, the decrease in the density of the pancreatic branches of the vagus nerve in the islets was positively correlated with the intraepidermal small nerve fiber density. Thus, a decrease in vagal nerve density in the islets can be a phenotype of diabetic peripheral neuropathy. The intraepidermal small nerve fiber density can be used to predict beta cell volume. Decreases in vagal nerve density in the islets and in beta cell volume were also prevented by combination therapy with DPP‐4 and SGLT2 inhibitors. The combination of an SGLT2 inhibitor, which has strong effects on glycemic control, and DPP‐4, which has been shown to protect nerve and beta cell volume, may have a greater effect on beta cell volume than single‐drug administration through the preservation of nerve function.
SUMMARY

Recent advances in the pathological exploration of the pathogenesis of diabetes mellitus, particularly in the reduction of beta cell volume in type 2 diabetes mellitus and diabetic peripheral neuropathy, have been described. The inflammatory response is a common pathology in both pathologies. Our study also showed that a decrease in the nerve endings of the pancreatic branch of the vagus nerve can be directly associated with both pathologies. Although the prevalence of diabetes mellitus is currently showing a slight downward trend, a large proportion of the population is still affected by this disease; its pathophysiology and treatment, including complications, are not fully understood. Although biopsies are not performed for the diagnosis of diabetes mellitus, autopsy tissue analysis, which only pathologists can conduct, greatly contributes to the elucidation of the pathophysiology of diabetes mellitus. New medicines, such as double agonists of GLP‐1 and gastric inhibitory polypeptides, which are assumed to have more potent sterilizing and glucose‐lowering effects, are available on the market. In the future, further clarification of the pathogenesis and pathological changes in response to a new medicine via the use of new morphology‐based methods such as proteomics, spatiotemporal single‐cell analysis, and three‐dimensional structural analysis could be achieved. Based on these new findings, we hope to establish a curative therapy for diabetes mellitus, including its complications.
